questions.question: Explain why about 120 000 people of Japanese ancestry were removed from the West Coast in 1942.
questions.expected_answer: Long-standing anti-Asian racism (Issei barred from citizenship and land ownership, 1924 immigration ban) combined with fear and anger after Pearl Harbour, false rumours of spying, pressure from newspapers and economic competitors, and General DeWitt's view that ancestry determined loyalty. Intelligence reports (Munson, naval intelligence) found most were loyal but were ignored. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on 19 February 1942. The 1983 commission blamed race prejudice, war hysteria and failure of political leadership.

questions.question: Describe the removal process and conditions in the camps.
questions.expected_answer: Notices gave families about a week; they took only what they could carry and sold or lost property. They went to assembly centres such as Santa Anita racetrack stables, then to ten War Relocation Authority camps (e.g. Manzanar, Topaz, Heart Mountain) in remote areas. Families shared one room in tar-paper barracks behind barbed wire and watchtowers, with shared latrines, mess halls and harsh climate. People built schools, newspapers, gardens and sports. The 1943 loyalty questionnaire divided families; "no-no" respondents were sent to Tule Lake.

questions.question: Explain how Japanese Americans resisted or responded to internment and how the US government later acknowledged the injustice.
questions.expected_answer: Korematsu, Hirabayashi and Yasui challenged the orders in court; the Supreme Court upheld them (1943, 1944) though Endo (1944) ended detention of loyal citizens. Heart Mountain draft resisters demanded restored rights; others served in the 442nd and Military Intelligence Service. After a redress movement, the 1980 commission reported in 1983; Korematsu's conviction was overturned in 1983; the 1988 Civil Liberties Act apologised and paid 20 000 dollars to about 82 000 survivors.
